Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-2 January 23, 2025 Faculty Senate Meeting Context (from JCODL 2022-2023 final report): “Several years ago (circa 2013), URI adopted definitions of online and blended learning (Face to face [< 25% online], Blended [25-75% online], and Online [75-100% online]), with the implicit, but unstated, assumption that the online portion was asynchronous.
The COVID era of remote instruction gave rise to additional approaches to remote instruction and the need to reflect all available modality options and to provide clear, comprehensible and accessible definitions and descriptions for the benefit of faculty and students.” Rationale: The “adopted” definitions are not memorialized in the University Manual and the current need to update modality-related descriptions provides an opportunity to provide standardized language in the University Manual, where it will be easily found and understood.
The language is proposed for insertion into Chapter 8, Academic Regulations (Regulations for Students), Section 30, Courses.

Existing modalities will translate into new modalities as follows: 1. ‘In-person’ � ‘In-person’ 2. ‘Blended’ � ‘In-person and online asynchronous’ or ‘In-person and online synchronous’ 3. ‘Online’ � ‘Online synchronous’ or ‘Online synchronous and asynchronous’ or ‘Online asynchronous’.
Because current ‘online’ and ‘blended’ modality courses will need to be assigned to a new modality (perhaps more than one if multiple faculty teach the same course using different modalities), faculty/departments will be allowed to update the modality of current ‘online’ and ‘blended’ modality courses directly with the registrar without going through the standard course modification process.
A course change proposal will not be necessary if faculty/departments teaching a class in one of the three ‘in-person’ modalities (‘In-person’, ‘In-person and online asynchronous’, ‘In-person and online synchronous’) wish to adopt (or add, in the case of a multi-section class) another of the ‘in-person’ modalities.

A course change proposal will not be necessary if faculty/departments teaching a class in one of the three ‘online’ modalities (‘Online synchronous’, ‘Online synchronous and asynchronous’, ‘Online asynchronous’) wish to adopt (or add, in the case of a multi-section class) another of the ‘online’ modalities.
As per current practice, course change proposals will continue to be necessary for courses with one of the three ‘in-person’ modalities that wish to adopt (or add, in the case of a multi-section class) one of the three ‘online’ modalities.
This is also true for ‘online’ modality courses that wish to adopt/add an ‘in-person’ modality.
Because of the volume of required changes, the new modalities will take effect starting in the Fall 2026 semester.

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 PASTORE HALL, 51 LOWER COLLEGE ROAD, KINGSTON, RI 02881 USA, P: 401.874.2616 Faculty Senate Resolution 2024-2025-03 Faculty Senate Meeting of January 23, 2025 Resolution on the Implementation of Honors Contracts WHEREAS, following considerable self-study and significant input from external experts, the URI Honors Program has proposed the use of honors contracts at URI.
Honors contracts are formal agreements, facilitated by an honors program, between a student and instructor.
They allow students and instructors to enhance non-honors courses to an honors level through additional learner-directed work tailored to the “broader, deeper, and more complex” learning experiences advocated by the National Collegiate Honors Council (NCHC); and WHEREAS, contracts are recognized by over 60% of honors programs in the USA, where they foster community and ownership by enhancing the educational process and commitment to the programs’ success.
For example, work at the University Honors Program at the University of Kansas shows that honors contracts act as far more than stopgaps to address honors course shortages.

They can “facilitate access to honors, increases completion, democratize key aspects of the honors experience, provide students with structured avenues for building relationships with faculty members, and empower students to own their educational experiences”; and WHEREAS, honors contracts may be best understood as a form of an independent study, entered into voluntarily by both students and faculty, with a contract defining outcomes, deadlines, and assessment definitions for additional work related to the course materials; and WHEREAS, honors contracts provide flexibility for students to align their education with their interests and goals.
They also allow programs to meet student needs when student/faculty constraints or funding limitations preclude offering stand-alone honors courses that fit student interests and needs; and WHEREAS, Contracts provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility at institutions such as ours that are not able to field enough faculty, cannot provide an adequate number of honors courses, or do not have a large enough student body to fill honors sections.

Contracts can fill the gap and provide opportunities for the self-guided intellectual growth of students; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Faculty Senate of the University of Rhode Island calls for implementation of the following Honors Contracts Proposal.
This includes making the

recommended changes to the University Catalog and to the eCampus system used by Enrollment Services; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Honors Program is called upon to reflect these changes on their website and in all other promotional and outreach materials promulgated by the Program. The Program is also called upon to review Chapter 8 of the University Manual (Academic Regulations, Honors Program) in light of the Contracts Proposal and bring any recommended changes to the Faculty Senate expeditiously; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the authority to offer Honors Contracts enabled by this resolution shall not extend beyond the Fall 2025 semester; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that no instructor may participate in more than three Honors Contracts in a single semester. Adopted this 23rd day of January, 2025. ____________________________________________________________ T heodore Walls, URI Faculty Senate President

Many programs also forge partnerships with businesses and other organizations to help in curriculum development, provide real-world learning opportunities, and facilitate networking and job placements for graduates.

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION NOVEMBER 14, 2024 Graduate Council Report 2024-2025-02B At the November 4, 2024 meeting of the Graduate Council, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval. Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by The Faculty Senate PROGRAM MODIFICATIONS COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES: PhD Marine Affairs, Effective Spring 2025 Appendix A The proposed changes include changing the credential type to “Degree”, initiation date of Spring 2025, change in location to “Kingston”, and changing required course credits to 21 from 18 plus an additional 45 credits instead of 48 credits. We are adding a new core course requirement of MAF 521 Coastal Zone Law. We have created a 500 level version of MAF 482, which is MAF 583 Quantitative Methods in Marine Affairs. The MAF 583 requirement replaces the MAF 482 requirement, since PhD students are not able to count 400 level courses toward their degree requirements. MA Marine Affairs, Effective Spring 2025 Appendix B We are adding a new core course requirement of MAF 521 Coastal Zone Law and reducing the total number of electives from 15 to 12. We are requiring that nine of the elective credits be within Marine Affairs. We have created a 500 level version of our MAF 482 course, which is MAF 583 Quantitative Methods in Marine Affairs. The MAF 583 requirement replaces the MAF 482 requirement. We have removed the option for MAF 598 Masters Project in order to streamline course codes.

Faculty determined that all MAF graduate students should take the Coastal Zone Law course in order to develop expertise in domestic coastal law as part of their degree program. The addition of this core course replaced one free elective, thus the total number of required credits (39) remains the same. MMA Marine Affairs, Effective Spring 2025 Appendix C We are adding a new core course requirement of MAF 521 Coastal Zone Law and reducing the total number of electives from 15 to 12. We are requiring that 50% of elective credits be within Marine Affairs. This change ensures that graduates of the Master of Marine Affairs program have expertise in domestic coastal law. Change in electives ensures that students take electives from within the department. Proposed changes include initiation date of Spring 2025, location change to “Kingston”; admission requirements to 3 instead of 5 years of post-graduate equivalent experience with the removal of “in marine areas employment”.

Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate PROGRAM MODIFICATIONS COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES: BS Environmental and Natural Resource Economics, Effective Winter 2025 Appendix A College of Business added TMD to their programs and any course code offered by COB qualifies as concentration credits for our ENRE degree tracks (Green Markets and Sustainability option and Green Business double major).
We propose to add the TMD code to our existing list of accepted COB courses (ACC, BAI, FIN, MGT, MKT, SCA, INE).
BS Medical Laboratory Science, Effective Spring 2025 Appendix B The proposed change involves the addition of six courses that would qualify as "Professional Electives" towards the MLS degree.

Namely, the added courses are: BIO 331 (Parasitology), CMB 312 (Introductory Biochemistry Laboratory), CMB 332 (Medical and Public Health Microbiology Laboratory), CMB 353 (Genetics Laboratory), CMB 491 (Research in Cell and Molecular Biology), and PHP 405 (Fundamentals of Epidemiology).
The addition of these courses accomplishes two goals.
First and foremost, they provide addition al opportunities for students to cultivate lab skills in areas that are relevant to MLS (BIO 331, CMB 312, CMB 332, CMB 353 and CMB 491) as well as explore MLS-related fields (BIO 331, PHP 405) that represent potential career pathways with a MLS degree.
Second, these additional courses provide more flexibility for students to successfully complete the six credit "Professional Elective" requirement of the MLS major in a timely manner.
This is due to the fact that many of the previously approved professional electives have prerequisite course requirements and limited scheduling options (i.e. offered only during fall or spring semester), which can make it challenging for students to complete this degree requirement.

Green Markets & Sustainability (BS Environmental & Natural Resource Economics), Effective Spring 2025 Appendix C The Green Markets and Sustainability specialization within our ENRE major is part of a double major offered by ENRE and College of Business, called Green Business double major.
College of Business added TMD to their programs and any course code offered by COB qualifies as concentration credits for our ENRE degree tracks (Green Markets and Sustainability option and Green Business double major).
We propose to add the TMD code to our existing list of accepted COB courses (ACC, BAI, FIN, MGT, MKT, SCA, INE) for the Green Markets and Sustainability specialization within our major.
Geography Minor, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix D We are suspending the Geography minor.
Only three courses in Geography are currently offered and the faculty who teach them will be retiring in 2026.
We do not anticipate being able to offer enough courses in the future to maintain the minor.

COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCES: BA - Psychology, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix E PSY412 Health Promotion has now been approved to be a permanent course, and we wish to add it to the Topics category of courses offered to BA PSY majors (students are required to take three Topics courses).
Pre-Professional Exercise Science (BS Kinesiology), Effective Fall 2025 Appendix F Suspend admission to this specialization.
Both the Pre-Professional Exercise Science and Applied Exercise Science specializations will be replaced by a single Kinesiology option.
The new specialization includes all courses required in both of these previous specializations as professional electives, so courses will remain available as this is taught out.
Applied Exercise Science (BS Kinesiology), Effective Fall 2025 Appendix G Suspend admission to this specialization.
Both the Pre-Professional Exercise Science and Applied Exercise Science specializations will be replaced by a single Kinesiology option.
The new specialization includes all courses required in both of these previous specializations as professional electives, so courses will remain available as this is taught out.

NEW CERTIFICATES, MINORS, or SPECIALIZATIONS COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING: Minor - Biochemical Engineering, Effective Spring 2025 Appendix H The Biochemical Engineering minor introduces students to the fundamental chemistry and physics underlying biological processes.
Students will apply engineering principles in a biological context to control the interactions between and behavior of organic molecules, proteins, and other biomacromolecules.
With this minor, students will be prepared for industrial and research positions in the biotechnology and biomedical fields.
The Biochemical Engineering minor is comprised of a minimum of 18 credit hours, at least half of which must be earned at URI.
The required courses include two fundamental science courses (6 credits), two biochemical engineering fundamentals courses (6 credits), and two or more supporting courses (6 credits).
Up to 6 credits can double count towards a major (e.g., core courses).
Students declaring this major must earn a minimum grade point average of 2.00 in courses counted towards the minor.

Students will need to complete the Biochemical Engineering minor form and have it signed by the minor coordinator, department chair, and appropriate dean.
Students are responsible for meeting the prerequisite requirements for individual courses, as applicable.

The course requirements for the undergraduate biochemical engineering minor are as follows: Fundamental Science Courses (6 Credits): CHM 112 General Chemistry Lecture II BIO 110 Fundamentals of Biology Biochemical Engineering Fundamentals Courses (6 Credits): CHE 574 Biochemical Engineering I CMB 311 Introductory Biochemistry Supporting Courses (6 Credits): CHE 466 Biomaterials CHE 491/2 Special Problems (max 3 credits)* CHE 548 Separations for Biotechnology CHE 553 Bionanotechnology CHM 441 The Chemistry of Biological Systems CMB 210 Biochemical Aspects of Nutrition and Physiology CMB 341 Principles of Cell Biology CMB 421 Physical Biochemistry CMB 426 Structural Biochemistry CMB 482 Proteins and Enzymes CVE 472 Biosystems in Environmental Engineering PHY 430 Modern Biological Physics * Students must complete a research project related to biochemical engineering under the guidance of a faculty member and get prior permission from the Biochemical Engineering Minor Coordinator.
